job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Freya Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I finished my marketing degree, with a focus on analytics, in the summer and I live with my mum and my gran in a terraced house on Alder Street. A normal day is up at seven, a couple of hours using AI tools to draft and test pitches, then calls and freelance bits for two small online shops. In the afternoon I apply for full-time marketing jobs and tweak my portfolio site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of all that, and what part do you still like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hardest thing is that I'm busy all day and still have no salary. I've done maybe thirty applications and got a few first calls. What I still love is seeing a campaign report move: at my internship with a small e-commerce company called Brightloop I rewrote an email sequence and sales went up 12 percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for people like me who already know the tools, and that the panic was overblown. But I'd also say the firms hoarding the gains are the real story, not the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if it's mostly hype, then I'm in the same spot as every other graduate, with some debt and three weeks of savings. My edge is that I'm already faster with the tools, so I'd keep the small freelance income going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the two freelance clients and pitch a third in the first month. I'd apply for ten marketing jobs a week, and put a short case study on my site for each client, with the numbers. I'd also tell Brightloop I'm available part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, a bit like a Tuesday. I'm not excited, but I'm not scared, and I get a little restless when things don't move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI every day. How does that sit with the idea that it's hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daily AI use makes the work quicker, but it doesn't make anyone hire me. In a hype world the tools are a nice speed boost, and the barrier is the same tired thing: firms want three years of experience for an entry role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your gran say when she sees you working from the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My gran says I'm lucky to be working at a kitchen table, because her generation had to leave home to do anything. She says it with a wink, and then asks if I've eaten.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but oversold**, and the real story is firms hoarding the gains.
I'd tell friends my **freelance work** shows the tools help those who already use them.
think: If it's mostly hype, I'm in the **same spot** as other graduates, with some debt and thin savings.
My edge is that I'm **already faster** with the tools.
do: Pitch a **third freelance client** in the first month and publish case studies with real numbers.
Apply for **ten marketing jobs** a week and email my old internship about part-time work.
Keep my **freelance income** steady alongside the job hunt.
feel: It feels **fine, like a Tuesday**, though I get restless when things don't move.
S0.quote: Daily AI use makes the work quicker, but it doesn't make anyone hire me.
fieldNote: Freya has **some income** from freelancing, so her own money feels less shaky than most jobless graduates.
She is unbothered by the hype question and **blames firms** for hoarding gains.
The barrier she names is **experience requirements**, not technology.

steps.text: Pitch a third freelance client in the first month
Apply for ten marketing jobs every week
Write a data-backed case study for each client

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the moment to learn the tools and also demand rules, because workers shouldn't be the ones paying for firms swapping people for software. I'd post about it online, honestly, with examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of junior marketing roles shrink. Copywriting, reporting and basic ad testing are all things I do with AI in minutes. One person will do the job of three, and I want to be that one person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who builds AI workflows for small shops: automated reports, email sequences, simple chatbots. I'd package it as a monthly service and charge by results. At the same time I'd apply for roles that mention AI or automation in the title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and nervy at once. I like being early, but I know early only helps if there's a buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think the new jobs appear first in marketing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new roles are things like AI operations, content strategy with checking, and customer journey design. The jobs that vanish first are the junior writers and report-builders, which includes a lot of my friends from uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell friends who don't use these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them, one at a time, over a coffee. I'd say pick one boring task, like weekly reporting, and let the tool do the first draft while you fix it. Nobody learns this from a lecture.

say: I'd say learn the tools **and demand rules**, so workers don't pay for firms swapping people for software.
I'd post **examples online** of how I use AI at work.
think: Junior marketing roles will shrink, so one person will do **three jobs**, and I want to be that person.
Being early only helps if there's a **paying buyer**.
do: Build a **monthly AI workflow service** for small shops, with reports and email sequences.
Charge **by results** and put the numbers on my portfolio site.
Apply for roles with **AI or automation** in the title.
feel: It feels **exciting and nervy** at once.
S1.quote: One person will do the job of three, and I want to be that one person.
fieldNote: Freya treats the disruption as an **opening** but still sees her own grade of job shrinking.
She plans **a product**, not just a job hunt, which shows high adaptability.
Her worry is for **friends** who don't use the tools.

steps.text: Package AI reporting and email workflows as a monthly service
Apply for AI operations and automation roles
Show two friends one boring task done with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need big, fast action: a tax on AI profits, a basic income, and rules for workers. The big firms are going to make a fortune, and two years is far too short for a polite conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared for the whole market, even though I'm skilled. If AI does all thinking work, someone with my degree isn't special, and the clients I have could just use the tool themselves without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to build something that owns itself: a small online business or a tool, not a service that depends on hours. I'd cut my spending to the bone, put every freelance payment into savings, and move to a smaller place with my gran and mum. I'd also learn a hands-on skill, like cooking or electrical basics, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a cliff, and I'm a runner. I'm anxious, but I'd rather run than sit and watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum say about this, and what do you say back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say, 'We'll manage, we always do,' and I'd say that's what everyone says before the rent goes up. Then we'd sit with a pen and paper and work out what she and gran earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the two-year picture, what do you do differently from the other pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture I'd stop applying for jobs at big firms, since they're going to shrink anyway. I'd put the time into the tiny business and a backup trade instead.

say: I'd say we need **fast action**: a tax on AI profits and a basic income.
I'd say two years is **too short** for a polite conversation.
think: If AI does all thinking work, my degree **isn't special** and clients could skip me.
I'm anxious, but I'd **rather run** than sit and watch.
do: Build a **small online business** that doesn't depend on my hours.
Put **every freelance payment** into savings and live very cheaply with my mum and gran.
Learn a **hands-on backup skill** such as electrical basics.
feel: It feels like a **cliff**, but I'm a runner, not a watcher.
S2.quote: I'd use the two years to build something that owns itself
fieldNote: Freya's **adaptability** keeps her from panic, though her degree may lose its edge.
She links her plan to **household finances** with her mum and gran.
Her backup trade shows she takes the **robot gap** seriously.

steps.text: Build a small online business that doesn't depend on my hours
Save every freelance payment and live cheaply at home
Learn electrical basics as a hands-on backup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a different system if we start straight away, with retraining accounts and shorter work weeks. I'd say that to anyone who'll listen, and online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be a bit nervous, but I think I'm on the right side of it. I'd have time to take a first job in AI-heavy marketing, learn how firms actually deploy it and then start something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a salaried job for two or three years, save about half, and keep one freelance client. Then I'd launch my own agency-style business around 2029, aimed at small family firms who'll need help. I'd also join a union or professional group for people in digital work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a start line. I'm a bit keyed up, and I'd probably sleep okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What's the one thing you'd do with that extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra time is for getting paid to learn. In two years I'd be improvising. In five, I'd have a real employer teaching me how things work inside and a pay cheque to build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want politicians to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Politicians should fund retraining accounts and make firms disclose when they replace people. Boring stuff, but it'd help my mum's friends as much as me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to build** a different system, with retraining accounts and shorter weeks.
I'd say it to anyone who'll listen, **including online**.
think: I'm a bit nervous but on the **right side of it**.
A **first salaried job** would let me learn how firms really use AI.
do: Take a **salaried job** for two or three years and save about half.
Keep **one freelance client** and launch my own small agency around 2029.
Join a **digital workers' group** or union for support.
feel: It feels like a **start line**, with me a bit keyed up but sleeping okay.
S3.quote: The extra time is for getting paid to learn. In two years I'd be improvising. In five, I'd have a real employer teaching me how things work inside
fieldNote: Five years lets Freya **swap running for building**: job first, own business later.
Her mood falls to **uneasy** because she sees a route and has some income.
She shows concern for **people around her**.

steps.text: Take a salaried marketing job for two or three years
Save half of every pay cheque
Launch my own small agency around 2029
Join a union for digital workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair transition, as long as we use it. I'd tell people to get started now rather than wait for a perfect plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I feel quite calm. I'd have a decade to get a job, pay my debt, start a business and learn each wave of tools as it arrives. I know I'm lucky to be someone who enjoys the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job, learn the business side, and start my own thing by 25 or 26. I'd also invest a little each month into a basic index fund, since I'd want money in assets rather than just my own labour. I'd keep learning new tools every few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, and a bit abstract. I don't feel scared, just curious about what the world looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how do you see your career going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be running a small consultancy for firms adopting AI, or in a product role. By the time full AGI is here I'd want assets, savings and a network, not just a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in feeling relaxed about ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The risk is that I get cocky. I could assume I'll always adapt, and then one wave comes that I can't ride, and I have no cushion. So I'd keep saving even when it feels unnecessary.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for a **fair transition** if we use it.
I'd tell people to **start now** instead of waiting for a perfect plan.
think: I feel **quite calm**, since I'd have a decade to build skills, savings and a business.
I know I'm **lucky** to enjoy change.
do: Take a **first job** and learn the business side before starting my own thing by 26.
Put a little into an **index fund** every month to own assets.
Learn **new AI tools** every few months.
feel: It feels **exciting and abstract**, with more curiosity than fear.
S4.quote: By the time full AGI is here I'd want assets, savings and a network, not just a job title.
fieldNote: Freya's calm is **earned**, not a way of ignoring the risk.
She names her own **overconfidence** as the danger and plans a cushion.
She treats the decade as a chance to **own assets**, not just work.

steps.text: Take a first marketing job and learn the business side
Invest monthly in a basic index fund
Learn a new AI tool every few months
Start my own consultancy by age 26

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, definitely. Everything I'm building takes time, and two years is too short to get to the point where a business stands on its own. What would help is a proper income floor and cheap training that's open to everyone, not only people who already use the tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that the people who already use AI every day aren't the winners by default, because the ones who own the companies are. I'd like young people to see that and not blame themselves.

headlineQuote: The people who already use AI every day aren't the winners by default, because the ones who own the companies are.
portrait: Freya is a 23-year-old **marketing analytics graduate** living with her mum and gran on Alder Street, with no full-time offer yet.
She uses AI every day and earns **small freelance income** from two online shops, with some debt and thin savings.
She leans left, blames firms for hoarding gains, and wants an **income floor** and shared retraining.
Her moods run from uneasy to anxious and then calm, because she **builds her own routes** whenever the time allows.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, since a business needs more than two years to stand alone.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **income floor** and cheap, open training that isn't only for people who already use AI would help.
